## K-Means Algorithm Study Notes

### 1. Introduction

K-Means is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm used for partitioning a dataset into **K** distinct, non-overlapping clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: DEFINITION]. Each data point is assigned to the cluster with the nearest mean, also known as its centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: DEFINITION]. It is classified as a centroid-based, flat (non-hierarchical) clustering method [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: DEFINITION]. The algorithm works by iteratively assigning each point to the closest cluster centroid and then recalculating the centroids, repeating this process until assignments stabilize [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: DEFINITION]. A key characteristic of K-Means is that the number of clusters, **K**, must be specified before the algorithm is run [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: KEY IDEA]. The "best" clustering is achieved when the total squared distance between points and their assigned centroids is minimized [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 1.1 Key Idea].

### 2. Key Concepts

#### 2.1 The Objective Function (WCSS)
K-Means aims to minimize the **Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS)**, also known as **inertia** [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 1.2 The Objective Function]. This value represents the sum of squared distances between each point and the centroid of its assigned cluster [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 1.2 The Objective Function]. A lower WCSS indicates that points are closer to their centroids, resulting in tighter and more compact clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 1.2 The Objective Function].

#### 2.2 The K-Means Algorithm (Lloyd's Algorithm)
The K-Means algorithm, also referred to as **Lloyd's Algorithm**, follows a step-by-step procedure:
*   **1. Choose K:** Select the desired number of clusters, **K** [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure].
*   **2. Initialize Centroids:** Randomly initialize **K** centroids, often by picking **K** random data points or using K-Means++ [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure].
*   **3. Assignment Step:** Assign every data point to the nearest centroid, typically using Euclidean distance, thereby forming **K** clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure].
*   **4. Update Step:** Recompute each centroid as the mean of all points currently assigned to its respective cluster [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure].
*   **5. Repeat:** Steps 3 and 4 are repeated until the centroids no longer change significantly (convergence) or a maximum number of iterations is reached [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure].

The algorithm always converges (WCSS never increases between iterations), but it may converge to a **local minimum** rather than the global optimum, depending on initialization [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: EXAM TIP]. Convergence is reached when either cluster assignments stop changing or centroid positions stop changing within some tolerance [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: EXAM TIP].

#### 2.3 Distance Metric
K-Means conventionally uses **Euclidean distance** to measure the closeness between a data point and a centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.2 Distance Metric]. This is because the update step, which uses the arithmetic mean, is mathematically tied to Euclidean distance [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.2 Distance Metric].

#### 2.4 Centroid Initialization
Different methods exist for initializing centroids:
*   **Random (Forgy method):** K data points are picked at random from the dataset to serve as initial centroids [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.3 Centroid Initialization].
*   **Random Partition:** Each point is randomly assigned to one of K clusters, and then initial centroids are computed as the means of these clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.3 Centroid Initialization].
*   **K-Means++:** This method chooses centroids one at a time, with each subsequent centroid chosen with a probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.3 Centroid Initialization]. This strategy helps spread out initial centroids and improves convergence [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.3 Centroid Initialization].

Poor initialization can lead K-Means to converge to a suboptimal local minimum [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: WHY IT MATTERS]. To mitigate this, the algorithm is often run multiple times with different random initializations (e.g., `n_init=10` in scikit-learn), and the run with the lowest WCSS is selected [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: WHY IT MATTERS].

#### 2.5 Choosing the Optimal Number of Clusters (K)
Since K must be chosen in advance, selecting an appropriate value is crucial [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4. Choosing the Optimal Number of Clusters (K)]. Two common techniques are:

*   **Elbow Method:** K-Means is run for a range of K values (e.g., 1 to 10), and the WCSS is recorded for each [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.1 The Elbow Method]. A plot of K against WCSS is then generated. As K increases, WCSS always decreases, but the rate of decrease slows down after the "true" number of clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.1 The Elbow Method]. The point where the curve bends sharply, resembling an "elbow," suggests a good value for K [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.1 The Elbow Method].
    ![Infographic - Elbow Method for K-Means](http://localhost:8001/static/generated_content/ml/k-means/notes/v1_http://localhost:8001/static/generated_content/ml/k-means/notes/v1_infographic.png)
    The "elbow" marks the K beyond which WCSS reduction flattens out significantly [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.1 The Elbow Method].

*   **Silhouette Score:** This metric quantifies how well each point fits within its assigned cluster compared to other clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score].
    *   A score close to **+1** indicates the point is well-matched to its own cluster and far from others, signifying good clustering [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score].
    *   A score close to **0** suggests the point lies near the boundary between two clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score].
    *   A score close to **-1** implies the point is likely assigned to the wrong cluster [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score].
    The average silhouette score across all points is computed for each candidate K, and the K with the highest average score is generally preferred [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score]. The Elbow Method is visual and subjective, while the Silhouette Score provides an objective quantitative measure [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: EXAM TIP].

#### 2.6 K-Means++ Initialization Procedure
K-Means++ is a smarter initialization strategy to overcome the limitations of standard random initialization [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5. K-Means++ Initialization]. Its procedure is:
*   **1.** Choose the first centroid uniformly at random from the data points [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5.1 K-Means++ Procedure].
*   **2.** For each remaining data point, compute its squared distance to the nearest already-chosen centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5.1 K-Means++ Procedure].
*   **3.** Choose the next centroid randomly, with a probability proportional to this squared distance; points farther from existing centroids are more likely to be chosen [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5.1 K-Means++ Procedure].
*   **4.** Repeat steps 2–3 until all K centroids are chosen [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5.1 K-Means++ Procedure].
*   **5.** Proceed with standard K-Means assignment/update steps [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 5.1 K-Means++ Procedure].
This method helps by spreading initial centroids further apart, reducing the chance of poor local minima, leading to faster convergence and better quality clustering [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: WHY IT HELPS].

#### 2.7 Advantages and Limitations
**Advantages:**
*   Simple to understand and implement [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Computationally efficient, scaling well to large datasets [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Works well when clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Guaranteed to converge (WCSS decreases monotonically) [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Easily parallelizable [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].

**Limitations:**
*   Must specify K in advance [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Sensitive to initial centroid placement, potentially converging to a local minimum [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Assumes clusters are convex/spherical and similar in size, struggling with irregular shapes [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Sensitive to outliers, which can pull centroids away from true cluster centers [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].
*   Sensitive to feature scaling; features with larger ranges can dominate distance calculations, requiring standardization/normalization [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].

#### 2.8 K-Means vs. Hierarchical Clustering
| Aspect                  | K-Means                                                              | Hierarchical Clustering                                          |
| :---------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Number of clusters (K)** | Must be specified in advance                                         | Not required in advance; chosen after viewing dendrogram         |
| **Output**              | A single flat partition                                              | A complete hierarchy / dendrogram                                |
| **Reproducibility**     | Depends on random centroid initialization                            | Deterministic (same result every run)                            |
| **Scalability**         | Scales well to large datasets — O(n · K · i)                         | Poor for very large datasets — O(n²) or worse                    |
| **Cluster shape**       | Assumes roughly spherical, equally-sized clusters                    | Can capture nested, non-spherical structures (depending on linkage) |
| **Sensitivity to outliers** | Sensitive — outliers distort centroids                               | Single linkage sensitive; Ward's/complete linkage less so        |
[Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 7. K-Means vs Hierarchical Clustering]

#### 2.9 Real-World Applications
K-Means is applied in various domains:
*   **Customer Segmentation:** Grouping customers by purchasing behavior for targeted marketing [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].
*   **Image Compression:** Reducing the number of distinct colors in an image by clustering pixel colors [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].
*   **Document Clustering:** Grouping similar documents or articles by topic [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].
*   **Anomaly Detection:** Flagging points far from any centroid as potential outliers [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].
*   **Geographic/Spatial Analysis:** Identifying regional clusters, e.g., for delivery hub placement [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].
*   **Recommendation Systems:** Grouping users with similar preferences for collaborative filtering [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 8. Real-World Applications].

### 3. Formulae

*   **Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) / Inertia:**
    WCSS = Σᵢ<sub style="font-size: 0.7em;">=1</sub><sup>K</sup> Σ<sub>x ∈ Cᵢ</sub> ‖x − μᵢ‖²
    where Cᵢ is cluster i, and μᵢ is the centroid (mean) of cluster i [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 1.2 The Objective Function].

*   **Euclidean Distance:**
    d(x, μ) = √Σ(xⱼ − μⱼ)²
    This measures closeness between a point `x` and a centroid `μ` [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 2.2 Distance Metric].

*   **Silhouette Score for a point x:**
    s(x) = (b(x) − a(x)) / max(a(x), b(x))
    where `a(x)` is the average distance from x to other points in its own cluster, and `b(x)` is the average distance from x to points in the nearest neighboring cluster [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 4.2 Silhouette Score].

*   **Computational Efficiency:**
    O(n · K · i · d)
    where `n` = number of points, `K` = number of clusters, `i` = number of iterations, and `d` = number of dimensions/features [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 6. Advantages and Limitations].

### 4. Examples

#### Worked Numerical Example: Clustering 6 One-Dimensional Points
Consider 6 one-dimensional points: **2, 4, 10, 12, 3, 20**. We will cluster them into **K = 2** clusters using K-Means [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3. Worked Numerical Example].

**3.1 Step 1: Initialize Centroids**
Suppose we randomly pick the initial centroids as **µ₁ = 2** and **µ₂ = 10** [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.1 Step 1: Initialize Centroids].

**3.2 Step 2: Iteration 1 — Assignment**
Each point is assigned to the nearest centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.2 Step 2: Iteration 1 — Assignment].

| Point | Distance to µ₁ (2) | Distance to µ₂ (10) | Assigned Cluster |
| :---- | :----------------- | :------------------ | :--------------- |
| 2     | 0                  | 8                   | C1               |
| 4     | 2                  | 6                   | C1               |
| 10    | 8                  | 0                   | C2               |
| 12    | 10                 | 2                   | C2               |
| 3     | 1                  | 7                   | C1               |
| 20    | 18                 | 10                  | C2               |
[Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.2 Step 2: Iteration 1 — Assignment]

**3.3 Step 3: Iteration 1 — Update Centroids**
Centroids are recomputed as the mean of points in their assigned clusters [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.3 Step 3: Iteration 1 — Update Centroids].
*   C1 = {2, 4, 3} → new µ₁ = (2+4+3)/3 = 3 [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.3 Step 3: Iteration 1 — Update Centroids].
*   C2 = {10, 12, 20} → new µ₂ = (10+12+20)/3 = 14 [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.3 Step 3: Iteration 1 — Update Centroids].

**3.4 Step 4: Iteration 2 — Re-Assignment**
Points are re-assigned based on the new centroids [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.4 Step 4: Iteration 2 — Re-Assignment].

| Point | Distance to µ₁ (3) | Distance to µ₂ (14) | Assigned Cluster |
| :---- | :----------------- | :------------------ | :--------------- |
| 2     | 1                  | 12                  | C1               |
| 4     | 1                  | 10                  | C1               |
| 10    | 7                  | 4                   | C2               |
| 12    | 9                  | 2                   | C2               |
| 3     | 0                  | 11                  | C1               |
| 20    | 17                 | 6                   | C2               |
[Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.4 Step 4: Iteration 2 — Re-Assignment]

The cluster assignments are unchanged from iteration 1 (C1 = {2,4,3}, C2 = {10,12,20}), indicating that the centroids will not move further [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.4 Step 4: Iteration 2 — Re-Assignment]. The algorithm has converged [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.4 Step 4: Iteration 2 — Re-Assignment].

**3.5 Final Result**
The final clusters are: C1 = {2, 3, 4} with centroid 3, and C2 = {10, 12, 20} with centroid 14 [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 3.5 Final Result].

### 5. Summary

K-Means is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that partitions data into **K** flat (non-nested) clusters based on the nearest centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision]. Its primary objective is to minimize the **Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS)**, also known as inertia, which represents the total squared distance between each point and its assigned cluster centroid [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision]. The algorithm operates through an iterative process, alternating between an **assignment step** (assigning points to the closest centroid) and an **update step** (recalculating centroids as the mean of assigned points) until convergence is achieved [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision].

The number of clusters, **K**, must be specified in advance, with common techniques for selection including the **Elbow Method** and the **Silhouette Score** [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision]. To improve initialization and reduce the risk of converging to poor local minima, **K-Means++** is often used, which strategically spreads initial centroids apart [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision]. While K-Means is fast and scalable (O(n·K·i)), it assumes spherical, similarly-sized clusters and is sensitive to outliers and feature scaling [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision]. The algorithm is guaranteed to converge, but it may converge to a **local** minimum, making multiple random initializations a recommended practice [Source: K_Means.pdf, Page: 1, Section: 9. Summary & Quick Revision].
